steps.say: Twisted gut hides far more often than it strikes. Most rotational quirks never cause trouble, yet nine in ten true cases declare themselves in the first year, and a rare few wait until adulthood.
steps.tx: Twisted gut hides in plain sight. Rotational anomalies reach **2 to 5 per 1000 births** (two to five per thousand births) at autopsy, yet clinical **malrotation** (twisted gut fixation) disease is **1 in 6000** (one in six thousand), with an **incidence** (new case rate) far below the anatomy rate. **90 percent** (ninety percent) present before **12 months** (twelve months), while up to **1 percent** (one percent) bring an **adult presentation** (grown up first twist) with chronic unexplained pain.

steps.say: When the gut never finishes its turn, the whole middle bowel hangs on a narrow hinge around its main artery. Babies born with wall or diaphragm defects deserve a rotation check too.
steps.tx: Failed turning leaves a lethal hinge. Failed **fixation** (gut anchoring) leaves the duodenojejunal and ileocecal junctions close together on a narrow **mesenteric stalk** (gut hinge) around the **superior mesenteric artery** (main gut artery) that twists easily. Associated defects include diaphragmatic hernia, gastroschisis and omphalocele, so a baby with one wall or diaphragm defect earns a rotation check too.

steps.say: Green vomit in a sleepy newborn means a twisted gut until proven otherwise. Do not sedate and watch; resuscitate and move, because intermittent cramps with black stools or a swollen acidotic belly each warn of dying bowel.
steps.tx: Green vomit in a newborn is volvulus until proven otherwise. Acute **bilious emesis** (green vomiting) in a lethargic newborn is ominous for **midgut volvulus** (twisted middle gut), while intermittent crampy pain with malabsorption and melena marks partial twists, and a distended abdomen with acidosis signals life threatening **intestinal ischemia** (dying gut). Never sedate and watch a green vomiter; resuscitate and move.

vis.alt: Illustration of acute intestinal obstruction with dilated proximal bowel, fibrous band, collapsed distal bowel and an X ray inset with air fluid levels.
vis.caption: Obstruction physiology with dilated proximal and collapsed distal bowel. In midgut volvulus the choke point is the twisted stalk, and green vomit in a sleepy newborn means theatre. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: A stable baby earns one definitive dye picture showing a pointed cutoff or spiral taper in the low duodenum. Never let scans delay theatre when the child is sick.
steps.tx: Stable babies earn one definitive picture. **Upper GI contrast** (swallow dye test) is the study of choice in stable patients, showing a **bird beak** (pointed cutoff) in the **3rd part** (third part) of the duodenum or a **corkscrew sign** (spiral taper). Reversed superior mesenteric vein and artery on ultrasound supports the call, but never let scans delay theatre in a sick child.

steps.say: A sick twisted child skips every queue and goes straight to theatre with fluids running on the way. Each minute of strangled blood supply costs bowel length.
steps.tx: A sick twisted child skips every queue. An acutely ill child with suspected volvulus goes straight to **emergency laparotomy** (urgent belly opening) with **resuscitation** (fluids and support) en route, because every minute of ischemia costs bowel length and **bowel salvage** (saved gut) decides between normal life and short gut dependence.

steps.say: One operation from nineteen thirty six still rules today, with six steps in a fixed order. Untwist, cut the tethering sheets, straighten, widen the base, remove the appendix and lay everything flat.
steps.tx: One 1936 operation still rules today. The **Ladd procedure** (untwist and splay operation) untwists the mesentery, divides **Ladd bands** (tethering sheets) from right colon to side wall, straightens the duodenum, opens the mesenteric base across the vein, removes the appendix through **appendectomy** (appendix removal), and lays the bowel broad and flat with the cecum in the left upper quadrant. Memorise the order; examiners love it.

vis.alt: Diagram of Ladd bands tethering the duodenum to the caecum beside a pyloromyotomy panel showing hypertrophied pylorus with bulging mucosa.
vis.caption: Ladd bands tethering duodenum to caecum, divided at operation before the bowel is laid broad and flat. The left panel shows pyloromyotomy, a different newborn operation. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Stitching the bowel to the wall adds nothing, so skip it. Recheck doubtful bowel the next day, warn parents that twisting can return, and remember this disease feeds the short gut clinic.
steps.tx: What not to sew matters after. Suturing cecum or duodenum to the wall has no proven benefit, borderline bowel earns a **second look laparotomy** (recheck opening) at **24 to 36 hours** (twenty four to thirty six hours), **recurrence** (returning twist) reaches **10 percent** (ten percent), and volvulus causes about **18 percent** (eighteen percent) of paediatric **short bowel syndrome** (short gut dependence). A planned recheck beats a hopeful closure.

steps.say: After a good Ladd repair, prove the downstream pipe is open by passing a tube past the stomach outlet. A hidden inner curtain can sit beside the twist, and missed dual blockage explains feeds that never advance.
steps.tx: One tube check prevents a missed second blockage. An **orogastric tube** (mouth to stomach tube) passed beyond the pylorus after Ladd repair excludes a coexisting **duodenal web** (inner curtain blockage), since dual pathology is described as an **associated anomaly** (paired defect). If feeds still fail to advance after a good Ladd, think web before blaming the twist repair.
